name: Myofunctional therapy

lead: Orofacial myofunctional therapy is a set of exercises for the tongue, lips, cheeks and throat muscles. Clinics use it for obstructive sleep apnea, tongue dysfunction and open bite, and looksmaxxers discuss it alongside tongue posture and mewing in hopes of better jaw and facial development.

The exercises aim to change the tone and function of the oral and upper-airway muscles. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined it for obstructive sleep apnea in children and adults, and other studies look at its use with CPAP and in orthodontic cases. The evidence concerns airway and function; none located tests it for facial appearance.

paras: People follow a structured program of daily exercises, often guided by a therapist, over weeks to months. In looksmaxxing circles it is paired with tongue posture practice.
No notable risks are described in the sources consulted. Sleep apnea is a medical condition managed by clinicians.

angle.text: Better tongue posture and airway function that followers hope translates into jaw and facial change. Mouth and tongue exercises are used clinically for sleep apnea and tongue dysfunction. Studies measure airway outcomes; none has tested facial appearance.

lead: Orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT) is a program of exercises for the tongue, lips, cheeks and throat muscles, used clinically for conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea, tongue dysfunction and open bite [1][2]. People in looksmaxxing communities discuss it alongside tongue posture and mewing as a route to better jaw position, a clearer breathing pattern and a more defined lower face, though what is studied is function rather than looks [3][4].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of myofunctional therapy for obstructive sleep apnea examined polysomnographic, snoring and sleepiness outcomes in children and adults [1]. Further studies examine its use alongside CPAP, in children with sleep-disordered breathing, and in orthodontic cases [5][6][7][8]. Published research concerns airway and oral function; no trial located for this entry has tested facial appearance.

paras: Therapy programs promote changes in the musculature of the upper airway and mouth, and published reviews summarize the programs used and their possible mechanisms [2]. Typical programs combine tongue-strengthening and positioning exercises, lip and cheek muscle training, retraining of swallowing, and a shift towards nasal breathing, usually supervised over a series of sessions with home practice [2][8].
Outcome measures in studies include tongue elevation strength, resting tongue posture, swallowing pattern, snoring, daytime sleepiness and the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) from sleep studies [1][5][8].

A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies in children and adults [1]. In nine adult studies (120 patients) the authors report AHI falling from about 24.5 to 12.3 events per hour, a rise in lowest oxygen saturation, less snoring and lower Epworth sleepiness scores; in two pediatric studies (25 patients) AHI also decreased, and children who continued therapy after surgery stayed free of apnea over four years compared with controls [1]. The authors estimated reductions of roughly 50 percent in adults and 62 percent in children [1].

A European Respiratory Society guideline on non-CPAP therapies for sleep apnoea, developed with the GRADE approach, includes myofunctional therapy among seven options it addresses, alongside surgery, mandibular advancement devices, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and positional therapy [9]. A 2018 review describes the programs and proposed mechanisms [2].

A randomized trial registered as NCT01289405 assigned 100 men with obstructive sleep apnea to placebo therapy, myofunctional therapy, CPAP, or CPAP plus myofunctional therapy, with assessments after three months [5]. All treated groups had lower sleepiness and snoring, with the largest AHI reduction in the CPAP group. The myofunctional and combined groups improved tongue and soft-palate muscle strength relative to placebo, and the combined group used CPAP more than the CPAP-only group [5].

Studies have examined myofunctional reeducation in children with sleep-disordered breathing [6][7]. A pilot randomized trial of 22 children aged about 7 to 10 with anterior open bite and an immature swallowing pattern reported that OMT changed tongue elevation strength, resting tongue posture and tongue position during swallowing, with better tooth contact six months later; speech articulation did not change [8]. A further study examined relapse of open bites treated with appliances with and without therapy [10].

sections.h: Relation to mewing and tongue posture
paras: Mewing is named after British orthodontist John Mew, who developed the idea with his son Mike Mew as part of orthotropics, and holds that tongue-to-palate posture reshapes the jaws [4]. Wikipedia reports that interest rose on search and social platforms from January 2019, especially in looksmaxxing communities [4]. It describes mewing as unproven, reports that researchers have found no credible evidence for orthotropics, and notes that Mike Mew was struck off the UK dental register in 2024; the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw [4].

Clinical OMT is a separate, therapist-led discipline with its own research base in airway and swallowing function. Looksmaxxers sometimes group the two together, and some commentators distinguish them: OMT studies assess tongue function and breathing, whereas mewing claims concern bone structure [3][4].

On looksmax.org, users have asked whether jaw-growth devices and myofunctional exercises are pseudoscience, after a consultation that likened them to mewing [3]. The poster described clinicians claiming a few millimetres of forward movement through exercises and a device, linked to posture [3].

The studies cited do not report notable adverse effects from the exercises. Sleep apnea is a medical condition, and the guidelines cited place myofunctional therapy among several treatments to be chosen with a clinician [9][5].

Studies cited above cover sleep apnea, CPAP adherence, pediatric sleep-disordered breathing and open bite [1][5][6][7][8][10]. Reported results include lower AHI and snoring in adults and children, higher tongue strength and CPAP adherence in a randomized trial, and changes in tongue posture in children with open bite [1][5][8]. None located for this entry assessed facial appearance as an outcome.

timeline.event: Trial NCT01289405 of myofunctional therapy and CPAP in sleep apnea is registered; results published in 2017 [5].
Systematic review and meta-analysis reports reduced AHI after myofunctional therapy in adults and children [1].
Pilot randomized trial in children with anterior open bite and tongue dysfunction is published [8].
Review focusing on myofunctional therapy in obstructive sleep apnea is published [2].
Public interest in mewing and tongue posture rises sharply on social media [4].
European Respiratory Society publishes a guideline on non-CPAP therapies for obstructive sleep apnoea, including myofunctional therapy [9].
Mike Mew is struck off the UK dental register, according to Wikipedia [4].
